what_its_for: Lovastatin is used to lower your bad cholesterol (LDL) and fats (triglycerides) in your blood, and to raise your good cholesterol (HDL). It helps reduce your risk of heart attack, stroke, and other heart problems. It works best when combined with a heart-healthy diet and regular exercise.
how_to_take: Take lovastatin by mouth with a full glass of water. The regular tablet (Mevacor) should be taken with your evening meal, as your body makes more cholesterol at night. The extended-release tablet (Altoprev) should be taken at bedtime and swallowed whole — do not crush, chew, or break it. You can take it with or without food. Take it at the same time every day to help you remember.
dosing: The typical starting dose for adults is 20 mg once daily with the evening meal. Your doctor may adjust your dose over time based on your cholesterol levels. The maximum dose is usually 80 mg per day. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions — do not change your dose on your own.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember on the same day. If it is already the next day, skip the missed dose and take your next dose at the regular time. Do not take two doses at once to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store lovastatin at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C). Keep it away from heat, moisture, and direct light. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep this medicine out of reach of children and pets. Do not use it after the expiration date on the label.
what_to_avoid: Avoid eating grapefruit or drinking grapefruit juice while taking lovastatin, as it can increase the amount of medicine in your blood and raise your risk of side effects. Avoid drinking large amounts of alcohol, as it can increase your risk of liver problems. Do not take large doses of niacin (over 1 gram per day) without your doctor's approval. Tell your doctor about all other medicines you take, especially certain antibiotics, antifungals, HIV medications, or other cholesterol medicines, as these can cause dangerous interactions.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or seek emergency care if you experience: unexplained muscle pain, tenderness, weakness, or cramps (especially with fever or dark-colored urine — this could be a sign of a serious muscle problem called rhabdomyolysis); yellowing of your skin or eyes, dark urine, or severe stomach pain (possible liver problems); or an allergic reaction such as rash, hives, swelling of the face or throat, or difficulty breathing. Also tell your doctor if you become pregnant while taking this medicine.
when_it_works: You may start to see changes in your cholesterol levels within 4 to 6 weeks of starting lovastatin. Your doctor will check your cholesterol with a blood test after about 4 to 12 weeks to see how well the medicine is working. It is important to keep taking it even if you feel fine — high cholesterol usually has no symptoms, but the medicine is still working to protect your heart.
special_populations: Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Do NOT take lovastatin if you are pregnant or breastfeeding. It can harm an unborn baby or a nursing infant. Use effective birth control while taking this medicine, and tell your doctor immediately if you become pregnant. Children: Lovastatin may be used in children aged 10 and older who have inherited high cholesterol, but only under a doctor's supervision. Older adults (65+): Older adults may be more sensitive to muscle side effects. Your doctor will monitor you closely. Kidney or liver disease: Tell your doctor if you have kidney or liver problems, as your dose may need to be adjusted or this medicine may not be right for you.
